in_text_mentions: The basic problems in primary hyperoxaluria are caused by low solubility of Calcium oxalate (CaOx), which is deposited in the kidney and the urinary tract as nephrocalcinosis or urolithiasis [Figure 1A, B]. This leads to renal failure at which point, the increased production of oxalate is compounded by the failure to remove it from the body resulting in a very high corporeal oxalate load leading onto CaOx deposition all over the body. An international registry for hyperoxaluria is operational for these patients since 2004.[2]

in_text_mentions: An 18-year-old East Indian male was referred for consideration of renal transplantation. He presented with a 2-week history of vomiting and malaise, and a serum creatinine of 42.8 mg/dL requiring urgent hemodialysis. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial CT panel with white arrows indicates lumbar vertebral compression in the index case; the disease-focused article title plus caption manifestation and in-text diffuse bone involvement support attribution to primary hyperoxaluria/systemic oxalosis bone disease, though vertebral compression is a less specific and less common manifestation than nephrocalcinosis. B: Axial CT panel shows bilateral renal calcific densities indicated by arrows, directly matching the caption "nephrocalcinosis" and the in-text cortical nephrocalcinosis in a primary hyperoxaluria patient; nephrocalcinosis is a classic target-disease manifestation.
